title: Perturbation-Induced Linearization: Constructing Unlearnable Data with Solely Linear Classifiers
claim: Adding small imperceptible perturbations to clean training data makes models trained on it fail on clean test data, while models trained on clean data generalize.
layout: 3 panels left-to-right (data construction, DNN training, test accuracy), two parallel rows for clean vs unlearnable data, dashed arrow, arrows labeled Train/Test
description: Three hand-drawn, sketch-style panels read left to right. The left orange panel shows a stack of noisy, rainbow-colored perturbation images (labeled ×8/255) with a plus sign, combined with a stack of clean bird photos. A dashed curved arrow leads to a second stack labeled Unlearnable Data. Two parallel rows run through the figure. Each row has a Train arrow that goes into a neural-network diagram in the gray middle panel, green for the clean-trained model on top and pink for the unlearnable-trained model below. In the right green panel, Test arrows point from a stack of test bird photos to results. The top row shows a green check with 76.98% accuracy, and the bottom row shows a red cross with 3.14%. The contrast between the green and red outcomes draws the eye.
caption: Illustration of the workflow of unlearnable examples. DNNs trained on the unlearnable data perform poorly on the clean test data. Results are reported for PIL on ImageNet-100.
abstract: Collecting web data to train deep models has become increasingly common, raising concerns about unauthorized data usage. To mitigate this issue, unlearnable examples introduce imperceptible perturbations into data, preventing models from learning effectively. However, existing methods typically rely on deep neural networks as surrogate models for perturbation generation, resulting in significant computational costs. In this work, we propose Perturbation-Induced Linearization (PIL), a computationally efficient yet effective method that generates perturbations using only linear surrogate models. PIL achieves comparable or better performance than existing surrogate-based methods while reducing computational time dramatically. We further reveal a key mechanism underlying unlearnable examples: inducing linearization to deep models, which explains why PIL can achieve competitive results in a very short time. Beyond this, we provide an analysis about the property of unlearnable examples under percentage-based partial perturbation. Our work not only provides a practical approach for data protection but also offers insights into what makes unlearnable examples effective.
